content: Linalool is a naturally occurring terpene alcohol that is present in numerous flowers and spice plants. It is widely used in commercial applications, primarily due to its pleasant floral scent with a hint of spiciness. This compound is also known by other names, including β-linalool, linalyl alcohol, linaloyl oxide, p-linalool, allo-ocimenol, and 2,6-dimethyl-2,7-octadien-6-ol. In nature, over 200 plant species produce linalool. These plants are predominantly from the families Lamiaceae (such as mints and aromatic herbs), Lauraceae (including laurels, cinnamon, and rosewood), and Rutaceae (citrus fruits). Linalool is also found in birch trees and other plants across a wide range of climates, from tropical to boreal zones. Additionally, it has been identified in certain fungi. Linalool has a chiral center at the C3 position, resulting in two stereoisomers. The (S)-(+)-linalool isomer, also known as licareol, has the CAS number 126-90-9 (PubChem ID: 67179). The (R)-(–)-linalool isomer, referred to as coriandrol, has the CAS number 126-91-0 (PubChem ID: 13562). Both enantiomers occur naturally. For instance, (S)-linalool is a major component of the essential oils derived from coriander (Coriandrum sativum L., family Apiaceae) seeds, palmarosa, and sweet orange (Citrus sinensis Osbeck, family Rutaceae) flowers. On the other hand, (R)-linalool is found in lavender (Lavandula officinalis Chaix, family Lamiaceae), laurel (Laurus nobilis, family Lauraceae), and sweet basil (Ocimum basilicum, family Lamiaceae), among other plants. Each enantiomer elicits distinct neural responses in humans and is perceived as having a unique scent. In higher plants, linalool, like other monoterpenoids, is synthesized from isopentenyl pyrophosphate via the universal isoprenoid intermediate geranyl pyrophosphate. This process involves a class of membrane-bound enzymes known as monoterpene synthases. One such enzyme, linalool synthase (LIS), has been reported to produce (S)-linalool in various floral tissues. Linalool is widely used as a fragrance in household products such as soaps, detergents, shampoos, and lotions. It also serves as a chemical intermediate in industrial processes. A notable downstream product derived from linalool is Vitamin E. From a safety perspective, individuals with perfume allergies should avoid exposure to linalool, as it may trigger allergic reactions.
